read.sections.0.heading.back: No one makes everything all by themselves

read.sections.0.text.back: No one can make all the things they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person makes its paper, another person brings the notebook to the market and another person sells it. The things that people exchange are goods and services. Goods are things you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that someone does for other people, such as teaching, repairing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes goods or provides services. A consumer is a person who uses or buys them. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.
read.sections.0.text.source: No person can make everything they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person made the paper, another carried the notebooks to a market and another sold them. The things people exchange are goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that a person does for someone else, such as teaching, fixing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes a good or provides a service. A consumer is a person who uses or buys it. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: No one can make all the things they use. Think of a notebook. Many people help make and sell it. People exchange goods and services. Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: No one can make everything they use. Think of a notebook. Many people help to make it and sell it. People swap goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch, like rice. A service is work a person does for you, like teaching. A producer makes a good or does a service. A consumer uses or buys it. Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.

read.sections.1.text.back: Sometimes people exchange goods or services without using money. This is called the barter system. At Lakeside Market, Kofi exchanges some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi repairs Nadia's bicycle, and in return, Nadia helps Ravi's younger sister read. The barter system still happens in many places today. However, this system has a problem: both people must want what the other person owns, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use that money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and store value for later.
read.sections.1.text.source: Sometimes people swap goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside Market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's sister with reading. Barter still happens in many places today. However, it has a problem: both people must want what the other person has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and keep value for later.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Sometimes people exchange things without money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and Sara gives him eggs. Ravi repairs a bicycle, and Nadia helps his younger sibling read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other person has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell his fish to get money. Then he can buy rice.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Sometimes people swap things with no money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and she gives him eggs. Ravi fixes a bike, and Nadia helps his sister read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell his fish for money. Then he can buy rice.

read.sections.2.text.back: Every exchange depends on trust. The buyer believes that the food is fresh and its weighing is fair. The seller believes that the payment is genuine. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading. If people cheat, other people stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one of the reasons many markets have rules about fair weights and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. When people trade fairly, they can meet more of their needs, and communities become closer.
read.sections.2.text.source: Every exchange depends on trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh and the scales are fair. A seller trusts that the payment is real. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading. If people cheat, others stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair weights and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. When people trade fairly, they meet more of their needs, and communities become more connected.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Trade needs trust. The buyer believes the food is fresh. The seller believes the money is genuine. People believe other people will keep promises. If someone cheats, other people no longer trust them. Then trade becomes harder for all. Markets have long brought people together. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Trade needs trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh. A seller trusts that the money is real. People trust each other to keep a promise. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone. Markets have brought people together for a very long time. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.

write.example.back: In this exchange, Ravi gives Nadia a service. He repairs Nadia's bicycle. In return, Ravi's younger sister gets reading help from Nadia for a week. This exchange is barter because they exchange skills and no money is used. Trust helps because Ravi repairs the bicycle first. He trusts Nadia will keep her promise later. Without trust, Ravi might not help at all, and both of them would lose something useful.
write.example.source: In this exchange, Ravi gives Nadia a service. He fixes her bicycle. In return, Ravi's little sister gets help with reading from Nadia for one week. Without trust, Ravi might not help at all, and both of them would lose something useful.

watch.summary.back: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, this video reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, such as food, water and a place to live. Wants are things you would like to have, such as toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, such as food, books and toys. Services are work that people do for other people. A doctor helps people stay healthy. A pilot flies an aeroplane. A chef cooks food. Then this video gives some riddles. A book is goods, but a librarian provides a service when he/she helps you find a book. Pizza is goods, but delivering it to your house is a service.
watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, it reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, like food, water and a place to live. Wants are things you would like, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, like food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others. A doctor helps people stay healthy. A pilot flies a plane. A chef cooks food. Then the video gives some puzzles. A book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when they help you find one. A pizza is a good, but bringing it to your home is a service.

educatorNotes.0.back: The market, the food exchanges and the skill exchanges are deliberately made general. Partner organisations can rename Lakeside Market after a local market's name, use local foods and goods, and add skill exchanges that students see around them, such as help repairing things, sewing or translating.
educatorNotes.0.source: The market, the food swap and the skill swap are general on purpose. A partner can rename Lakeside Market after a local market, use local foods and goods, and add skill swaps that learners see around them, such as help with repairs, sewing or translation.

educatorNotes.1.back: This lesson does not say that barter always existed before money. Many historians and anthropologists question the idea that whole communities once lived by barter alone; gifts and credit were also common. Barter is shown as one way of exchanging that still happens today.
educatorNotes.1.source: The lesson does not say that barter always came before money. Many historians and anthropologists question the idea that whole communities once lived only by barter; gifts and credit were also common. Barter is shown as one way to exchange that still happens today.
